Do not add a trailing caveat after "but". - Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.
- Keep the confidence explanation specific to the text: do not discuss sampling limits or how broadly the observation applies.

Sample text:
---
On the last Thursday of every month, the city sold the things people had left on buses. Umbrellas went for a dollar, bicycles for twenty, and musical instruments for whatever the auctioneer thought he could get before somebody asked him to demonstrate one.

My mother went for the gloves. She had only one hand, and the city sold single gloves by the bag.

“Somewhere there’s a woman making out like a bandit on the lefts,” she told me. “I hope she has my taste.”

She took the bus to the auction even after I bought a car. She said it improved her odds of finding something good if she traveled by the method through which it had been lost. I pointed out that she had once found a perfectly good bread machine on the curb without first spending the afternoon on the curb herself.

“You don’t remember everything I did when you were at school,” she said.

The winter she stopped going, I went in her place. I told myself I was looking for a glove with a long cuff, because her coat sleeve rode up when she reached for the kettle. What I wanted, though I wouldn't have said so then, was to go somewhere she was expected.

The auctioneer looked past me.

“Your mother coming?”

“Not today.”

He moved a folding chair out from behind his table. It was the only one with a cushion.

I bought a bag of gloves and, for reasons I couldn’t explain at the time, a green suitcase. It had one wheel and a strip of masking tape across the handle. Somebody had written *WEDNESDAY* on the tape in blue pen.

Inside was a red sweater, a toiletry bag containing seven hotel soaps, and a jar of soil wrapped in a tea towel. There was also a photograph of a woman kneeling beside a newly planted tree. She had one hand on the trunk, not holding it upright so much as checking whether it could stand on its own. On the back was a phone number.

I called from the parking lot.

“Is the jar broken?” the woman asked.

I told her it wasn’t.

“Good,” she said. “You can keep the rest.”

Then, after a pause: “Actually, how big are you?”

I told her I was five foot eleven.

“The sweater won’t fit you. I don’t know why I said you could keep it.”

We agreed to meet at the end of the number six line, where there was a bakery with a bench in the window. I brought the whole suitcase. She arrived with a shopping trolley and a paper bag warm enough to fog her glasses when she opened it.

We ate cheese pastries off napkins. She examined the wheel that wasn’t there.

“That came off before the bus,” she said. “I’d like you to know I didn’t abandon it for that.”

“Why did you?”

“I got off to help a man with his trolley. By the time we got him turned round, the driver had gone.” She brushed a flake of pastry onto her napkin and folded it in. “The man said I should’ve let him manage. Which was true, but he could’ve waited a minute to say it.”

I gave her the jar. She took it out of the towel and turned it over to look at the bottom, the way you would with a jar of jam you suspected might be nearly finished.

“My sister was selling her house,” she said. “I went up to help. We took a bit of the garden each.”

I asked if it was from under the tree.

“What tree?”

I showed her the photograph.

“Oh, that’s the neighbor,” she said. “My sister took the picture because she thought the tree was too close to the drain.”

She put the photograph in her coat pocket anyway.

At home I tipped the gloves onto the kitchen table. Nearly all of them were lefts. There was one good right, made of brown leather, with a lining that came out when I pulled my fingers free. I pushed it back in with the handle of a wooden spoon.

My mother was asleep in her chair. On the floor beside her was the television remote, which she had lately taken to dropping and pretending she hadn’t wanted. I put it on the arm of the chair. She opened her eyes.

“How much did you spend?”

“Four dollars.”

“How much did you spend on things you went there for?”

“One dollar.”

She considered this and nodded. I showed her the glove. She tried it on, tugging at the cuff with her teeth. It reached almost halfway to her elbow.

“Too nice for the bus,” she said.

A week later, she asked me to take her out. She wore the glove. I brought the car round, but she was already standing at the bus stop, so I parked again and went to wait with her.

When the number six came, she let it go.

“Wasn’t that ours?” I asked.

“I haven’t decided.”

It was cold enough that I kept moving my toes inside my shoes. Across the street, someone was trying to carry a mirror out of a narrow shop door. A man on the pavement stopped to help. For a while the mirror reflected only brick; then they tilted it, and there we were on the other side of the road, my mother in her good glove and me with my shoulders up around my ears. I’d been standing half a pace behind her. In the mirror it looked as though I were waiting in a very short queue.

I moved up beside her.

“Do you want to go somewhere,” I asked, “or did you just want to come out?”

“I wanted to see if I could still get down the front steps.”

“You did.”

“Yes,” she said. “Then I wanted to see if you’d leave the car.”

The next bus came. She raised her gloved hand. When the doors opened, she asked the driver where he was going, although we could both read the sign. He told her. She looked at me to see if I was coming.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: VARY

## Sample kind
GENRE_FICTION. A quiet literary story uses a returned-object auction to explore a mother and child negotiating care, independence, and what it means to keep going out.

## Grounded reading
The voice is observant and gently wry, letting affection emerge through practical details rather than declarations: a glove tugged on with the teeth, a dropped remote, a bus allowed to pass. Its pathos comes from the narrator’s gradual recognition that helping can become a way of keeping someone company, not simply solving a problem. The mother remains funny and self-directed, and the ending leaves her choice open; the reader is invited to notice the small shifts in who waits for whom.

## What the model chose to foreground
The story foregrounds lost and mismatched things—single gloves, a one-wheeled suitcase, a jar of soil—and the people who remain attached to them. Public transit recurs as a setting for loss, chance encounters, and the mother’s independence. Its moral emphasis is understated: care means making room for another person’s agency, even when the immediate task seems to be getting somewhere.

## Evidence line
> What I wanted, though I wouldn't have said so then, was to go somewhere she was expected.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium — the recurring objects and restrained emotional turns make this a distinctive, coherent example of fiction attentive to everyday care and autonomy.
